content: The document titled Web Annex D: Modelling HIV self-testing for oral PrEP scale-up in Kenya: impact on HIV drug resistance and HIV outcomes is part of the World Health Organization's consolidated guidelines on differentiated HIV testing services. It explores the potential effects of using HIV self-testing (HIVST) as a strategy to facilitate the delivery of oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in Kenya, particularly in community-based settings. The study also examines the implications of this approach on HIV drug resistance and overall HIV-related health outcomes. The publication is made available under a Creative Commons license, allowing for non-commercial use, redistribution, and adaptation, provided proper citation is given. However, the use of the WHO logo is prohibited, and any adaptations must be licensed under the same or an equivalent Creative Commons license. If a translation of the work is created, it must include a disclaimer stating that the translation was not produced by WHO and that WHO is not responsible for its content or accuracy. The original English version remains the authoritative edition. The study was conducted by a team of researchers from institutions such as the University of Washington, the World Health Organization, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. It utilized an agent-based network model (EMOD-HIV) to simulate the scale-up of PrEP in western Kenya under four different HIV testing scenarios: (1) provider-administered nucleic acid testing (NAT), (2) provider-administered rapid diagnostic tests (Ab RDT), (3) blood-based HIV self-testing, and (4) oral fluid HIV self-testing. These scenarios were compared to a counterfactual scenario with no PrEP implementation. The study focused on individuals aged 18 to 49 years who had at least one sexual partner and tested HIV-negative, making them eligible for PrEP. The researchers assessed the cost and health impact of rapid PrEP scale-up using these different HIV testing modalities. Key findings include: A projected PrEP coverage of 29% could prevent 54% of HIV infections and 17% of HIV-related deaths among adults aged 18 to 49 over a 20-year period. The health impacts were similar across the different HIV testing modalities used to deliver PrEP. The proportion of drug resistance was low across all scenarios, including those using HIVST, when accounting for background NRTI resistance. The budgetary impact of implementing PrEP using HIVST and provider-administered RDT was comparable, while NAT was at least 50% more expensive. The study concludes that scaling up PrEP using HIV self-testing has comparable health impacts, costs, and a low risk of drug resistance when compared to provider-administered RDT. Stakeholders are encouraged to consider leveraging HIV self-testing as a means to expand PrEP access among populations at risk of HIV infection.
